title: Chocolate Biscotti
changes_from_base: 30 g cocoa replaces 30 g of the flour, a little more sugar, chocolate chunks with fewer almonds; judge doneness by a firm, cracked top rather than colour.
summary: These chocolate biscotti follow the classic almond biscotti method, with cocoa swapped in for some of the flour, a touch more sugar, fewer almonds and chocolate chunks folded through — judge doneness by the firm, cracked top rather than colour, since the dark dough makes golden edges hard to spot.
equipment: large metal baking tray lined with baking paper

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt
whole blanched almonds, toasted and roughly chopped

steps.title: Heat the oven
steps.text: Set the oven to 175°C (155°C fan) and let it heat for at least 20 minutes with a shelf in the middle. This recipe follows the same two-bake method as classic almond biscotti, but with cocoa replacing some of the flour and chocolate chunks standing in for most of the almonds. Because the dark dough won't turn visibly golden, you'll need to rely on texture and timing rather than colour to judge doneness.

steps.title: Whisk eggs and sugar
steps.text: Whisk the eggs, caster sugar, vanilla and salt together for about a minute until smooth and lightly frothy, then whisk in the cooled melted butter. The slightly higher sugar content in this version balances the bitterness of the cocoa. Whisking well at this stage dissolves the sugar evenly through the mixture.

steps.title: Bring in the dry ingredients
steps.text: Stir in the flour, cocoa powder and baking powder until a soft, sticky dough forms, then fold in the chopped almonds and chocolate chunks. Mix just until everything is evenly distributed, as overmixing at this point can toughen the crumb. The dough will look darker and slightly stiffer than a plain biscotti dough.

steps.title: Shape two logs
steps.text: With damp hands, shape the dough into two logs on the lined tray, each about 25 x 6 cm and 2 cm high, spaced roughly 8 cm apart. Keeping your hands wet stops the sticky, chocolatey dough from sticking to your fingers as you shape it. The gap matters, since both logs spread outwards as they bake.

steps.title: First bake
steps.text: Bake for 25-30 minutes, until the tops feel firm and have just started to crack across the surface. Because the cocoa masks the usual golden colour cue, lean on the firm, cracked top and the timing to tell you the logs are ready. Those surface cracks show the dough has set enough right through to slice cleanly.

steps.title: Cool before slicing
steps.text: Let the logs cool on the tray for 20-25 minutes before cutting. Slice them too soon and the warm crumb will crumble; wait until they're fully cold and they turn brittle enough to shatter instead. This resting window is when the logs are firm but not yet hardened, which makes for the cleanest cut.

steps.title: Lower the oven and slice
steps.text: Reduce the oven to 150°C (130°C fan) for the second bake. On a board, cut each log on the diagonal into 1.5 cm slices with a serrated knife, using a gentle sawing motion so the chocolate chunks don't tear the crumb as you cut. Diagonal slices also give you a larger surface area to dry out in the next step.

steps.title: Second bake to dry out
steps.text: Stand or lay the slices back on the tray and bake for 20-25 minutes, turning once, until they feel dry and firm rather than soft when pressed. This slower, lower-temperature bake drives out the remaining moisture for a proper biscotti snap. Again, judge by feel rather than colour, since the cocoa keeps the surface dark throughout.

steps.title: Cool completely
steps.text: Move the slices to a wire rack and leave them to cool fully. They firm up noticeably as they cool, so don't worry if they still feel slightly soft straight out of the oven. Makes about 30 biscotti.

tips: Judge this dough by feel and time, not colour — the cocoa hides the golden tones you'd normally look for, so a firm, cracked top is your real cue.
Chop the chocolate chunks a little larger than you think you need; they soften during baking and smaller pieces can mostly dissolve into the dough.
Don't slice the logs while they're still hot — a common mistake that crumbles the crumb; let them cool for the full 20-25 minutes first.
Use a gentle sawing motion rather than pressing straight down, as chocolate chunks can tear or crack the slice if you cut too forcefully.
If the dough feels too soft to shape, chill it for 10 minutes — cocoa can make dough slightly stickier than the classic version.
safety: Don't taste the raw dough or batter: raw flour and raw egg aren't safe to eat until baked.
storage: Store in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 2 weeks. These also freeze well for up to 3 months; thaw at room temperature before serving.
